title: Mystery Samples

beats.narrativeText: Deep in the station laboratory, a row of samples sits carefully catalogued — but whoever was labelling them never finished the job.
Atlas offers one warning before the learner touches a single sample: scientists classify by evidence, not by what something looks like at a glance — and that distinction is about to matter.
The learner works through the samples one at a time, observing their properties carefully rather than trusting a first impression.
Grouping the samples by what they actually share, rather than how they look side by side, starts to reveal a pattern nobody labelled for them.
The learner must record the evidence behind every grouping and be ready to justify exactly why each sample belongs where it does.
Every sample ends up classified using nothing but observable properties — no assumptions, no guessing from appearance alone.
The learner reflects on how differently the samples sorted out once evidence, rather than appearance, was doing the work.
With the samples finally classified, the laboratory's incomplete records start making sense — and they point toward another part of the expedition's research nobody has reached yet.

activities.title: Observe Sample Properties
activities.storyContext: Several samples sit carefully catalogued in the station laboratory — someone clearly meant to label them properly, and never got the chance.
activities.instructions: Observe each sample carefully and record its properties — colour, texture, size and any other details you can actually point to, not what you assume it might be.
activities.output: A list of observed properties for each sample.

activities.title: Group Similar Specimens
activities.storyContext: Atlas's warning still stands: classify by evidence, not by appearance alone — two samples that look similar at a glance won't always belong together.
activities.instructions: Group the samples into categories based on the properties you actually observed, not how they look sitting next to each other.

activities.title: Record Evidence
activities.storyContext: A classification nobody can check is barely better than a guess — clear records let a future Explorer verify your work without redoing it.
activities.instructions: Write up the specific evidence supporting each group you created.
activities.output: Written evidence records for each group.

activities.title: Justify Classifications
activities.storyContext: A good classification can always be explained using evidence — if it can't, it isn't really a classification yet.
activities.instructions: Explain why each sample belongs in its group, pointing directly to the evidence you recorded rather than restating your first impression.
activities.output: A justified classification for each sample.

activities.title: Design a Classification Key
activities.storyContext: A classification key would help future Explorers sort new samples quickly.
activities.instructions: Design a simple classification key that could sort new samples into your groups.

activities.title: How Biologists Classify New Species
activities.storyContext: Classifying unidentified samples is exactly the work real biologists do.
activities.instructions: Find out how biologists classify newly discovered species.
activities.output: None required — this is an open investigation.

prompts: What evidence did you use to classify the samples, and did any of them surprise you by not belonging where they looked like they should?

discussionPoints: Why is it important to classify by evidence rather than appearance alone?
What surprised you about grouping the samples?
parentGuide.assessment: Look for classifications justified by recorded evidence, not just first impressions.

completionCriteria: Sample properties observed, specimens grouped, and classifications justified with recorded evidence.
